newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia's Proton in high-tech and export drive.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia's Proton in high-tech and export drive.

text.p: Malaysian car maker Proton Bhd, with Britain's Lotus, France's Citroen and Japan's Mitsubishi already under its hood, said on Monday it will continue buying foreign auto technology to build up its exports.

"Our mission is to be a world-class automotive producer, a major export earner for the country and a leading Malaysian high-technology employer," Proton chairman Yahaya Ahmad said at the rolling-out ceremony of the company's one-millionth car.
Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad officiated the ceremony, at which Proton's sixth and newest model, the 1.8-litre Putra, was also unveiled.

Proton, Mahathir's brainchild, began making its range of three- and five-door sedans and sporty cars in 1985 through a joint-venture with Mitsubishi Corp and Mitsubishi Motors Corp under Malaysia's "Look East" policy. The Japanese have a joint 16.12 percent stake in Proton.
A second national car, the subcompact Kancil, was launched in 1994 between the local Perusahaan Otomobil Kedua Sdn Bhd and Japan's Daihatsu Motor Co Ltd and Mitsui Co Ltd

But a noticeable shift to Western technology was seen last year when Proton tied up with Automobiles Citroen to produce a variation of the Citroen AX coupe, and bought an 80 percent stake in sports car maker Lotus this year.
Both Yahaya and Mahathir said the collaboration with European car makers was not a snub of Mitsubishi for its alleged reluctance in the past to transfer technology to Proton.
"We are very happy with the relationship we have with Mitsubishi, but that by itself does not mean that we should be satisfied and cease looking at alternative sources of technology," Yahaya said.
He said the company was looking for joint-venture partners where Proton could have "a full controlling stake, or a minority stake where we can play a meaningful role".

Mahathir, who has blamed Mitsubishi for Proton's lack of knowledge in making its own engine and transmission parts, said negotiations were under way for Mitsubishi to make some of its main components in Malaysia and import them back into Japan.
The price of the cheapest Proton has jumped by more than 100 percent in the last 11 years and Mahathir said the car would not be competitive overseas if this trend continued.
"The Japanese would also stand to gain by producing their parts here as our operating costs are lower," he said.
Yahaya said Proton's goal was to produce a million cars a year and export about half of them.

The Malaysian car is now exported to 39 countries, with Britain being the largest buyer. Current production capacity is 180,000 units a year, 10 percent of which are exported while the company's domestic market share is 65 percent.
Yahaya said a 2.0 billion ringgit ($793.7 million) factory planned by Proton in the northern Malaysian state of Perak will boost production to 260,000 units by the turn of the century.
